title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 832–834 (Night 183, continuing nights-182), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 183 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Bitten by Dahnash in the form of a flea, Qamar al-Zamān starts up from sleep, scratches his neck, and finds someone asleep beside him, sweeter-breathed than musk and softer than butter: the Lady Budūr, a girl like a pearl, praised in two short poems. He sees her in a Venetian shift with no drawers beneath it, her jewelled coif, earrings and necklace of matchless pearls, and is dazed; the vital heat stirs in him and God casts upon him the lust to couple with her. He opens the neck of her shift and gazes at her breasts, like two ivory caskets, and tries to wake her, but Dahnash has made her sleep heavy and she does not stir. He guesses that she must be the girl his father has wanted him to marry these three years, and resolves to tell his father in the morning to marry him to her, so that he may take his fill of her. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-third night,
sentences.n: al-thālitha, “the third”, agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ دَهْنَشًا انْقَلَبَ فِي صُورَةِ بُرْغُوثٍ وَقَرَصَ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ فَوَثَبَ مِنْ مَنَامِهِ مَرْعُوبًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu-anna Dahnashan inqalaba fī ṣūrati burghūthin wa-qaraṣa Qamara al-Zamāni fa-wathaba min manāmihi marʿūban
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Dahnash turned in(to the) form (of) a-flea and-nipped Qamar al-Zamān, and-he-leapt-up from his-sleep terrified.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Dahnash turned himself into the shape of a flea and bit Qamar al-Zamān, who started up out of his sleep in terror.
sentences.n: The print has موعوبا, a misprint for مرعوبا, corrected here: marʿūban, “terrified”, as in the same sentence at the end of the last night. Shahrazād takes up the story by repeating that sentence. السعيدان is set solid in the print, as in earlier nights: al-saʿīdu, “fortunate”, and anna, “that”, run together as one word, and it is pointed here across the join. دهنشا is written with the alif of the accusative ending -an, as if the name were fully declinable, and is pointed so, Dahnashan; a foreign name like this is ordinarily a diptote, Dahnasha, without tanwīn. inqalaba fī ṣūrati, “turned into the form of”. qaraṣa, “to pinch, nip”: of a flea, “to bite”. marʿūb, “frightened”, is accusative as a state (ḥāl).

sentences.t: وَهَرَشَ مَوْضِعَ الْقَرْصَةِ فِي رَقَبَتِهِ مِنْ شِدَّةِ مَا أَحْرَقَتْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-harasha mawḍiʿa al-qarṣati fī raqabatihi min shiddati mā aḥraqathu
sentences.l: And-he-scratched (the) place (of) the-bite in his-neck, from (the) intensity (of) what it-burned-him.
sentences.i: He scratched the spot on his neck where he had been bitten, so fiercely did it burn.
sentences.n: harasha, “to scratch (an itch)”, is the everyday word. qarṣa, “a nip, a bite”, is the noun of a single act (pattern faʿla) from qaraṣa. min, “from”, gives the cause: min shiddati mā aḥraqathu, “from the intensity of how it burned him”, where mā with the verb stands for a noun. aḥraqathu, from aḥraqa, Form IV, “to burn”, is feminine because its subject is the qarṣa.

sentences.t: فَتَحَرَّكَ بِجَنْبِهِ فَوَجَدَ شَيْأً نَائِمًا بِجَنْبِهِ وَنَفَسُهُ أَزْكَى مِنَ الْمِسْكِ الْأَذْفَرِ وَجِسْمُهُ أَلْيَنُ مِنَ الزُّبْدِ
sentences.tr: fa-taḥarraka bi-janbihi fa-wajada shayʾan nāʾiman bi-janbihi wa-nafasuhu azkā mina al-miski al-adhfari wa-jismuhu alyanu mina al-zubdi
sentences.l: And-he-moved with-his-side, and-found a-thing sleeping at-his-side, and-its-breath (was) sweeter than the-musk, the-pungent, and-its-body softer than the-butter.
sentences.i: He shifted onto his side, and found something asleep beside him, whose breath was sweeter than the strongest musk and whose body was softer than fresh butter.
sentences.n: bi-janbihi comes twice: first bi- is “with”, taḥarraka bi-janbihi, “he moved with his side”, he shifted his body over; then bi- is “at”, bi-janbihi, “at his side”, beside him. shayʾ, “a thing”, is masculine, and so are the pronouns after it (nafasuhu, jismuhu): he does not yet know what lies there. شيأ is the edition's spelling of shayʾan, with the hamza on an alif seat; the أ is printed, as is the ئ of نائما. nafas, “breath”: the fatha on the ف is the print's own, and keeps the word apart from nafs, “self”. azkā, elative of zakā, “to be pure”, of a scent “sweet”; min after it is “than”. misk adhfar, “musk of sharp, strong scent”. alyan, elative of layyin, “soft”. zubd, “fresh butter”.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ وَقَامَ وَجَلَسَ عَلَى حَيْلِهِ وَنَظَرَ إِلَى ذٰلِكَ الشَّخْصِ الرَّاقِدِ بِجَانِبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba Qamaru al-Zamāni min dhālika ghāyata al-ʿajabi wa-qāma wa-jalasa ʿalā ḥaylihi wa-naẓara ilā dhālika al-shakhṣi al-rāqidi bi-jānibihi
sentences.l: And-marvelled Qamar al-Zamān at that (the) utmost (of) the-marvelling, and-rose and-sat on his-strength, and-looked at that the-person, the-lying-asleep at-his-side,
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān marvelled at this beyond all measure. He raised himself and sat bolt upright, and looked at the figure sleeping beside him,
sentences.n: taʿajjaba min, “to wonder at”: min marks what causes the wonder. ghāyata al-ʿajabi, “the utmost of wonder”, is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) giving the degree. ʿalā ḥaylihi, “on his strength”: ḥayl is “strength, power”, and jalasa ʿalā ḥaylihi is the colloquial “sat right up”. shakhṣ, “a person, a figure”, still says nothing of sex. rāqid, “lying asleep”. bi-jānibihi, “at his side”: jānib is a synonym of janb.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَهَا صَبِيَّةً كَالدُّرَّةِ السَّنِيَّةِ أَوِ الْقُبَّةِ الْمَبْنِيَّةِ بِقَامَةِ النِّيَّةِ خُمَاسِيَّةَ الْقَدِّ بَارِزَةَ النَّهْدِ مُوَرَّدَةَ الْخَدِّ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadahā ṣabiyyatan ka-al-durrati al-saniyyati awi al-qubbati al-mabniyyati bi-qāmati al-niyyati khumāsiyyata al-qaddi bārizata al-nahdi muwarradata al-khaddi kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And-he-found-her a-girl like-the-pearl, the-resplendent, or the-dome, the-built, with-(a)-stature (of) the-intent(?), five-span (of) the-height, jutting (of) the-breast, rose-tinted (of) the-cheek, as said about-her the-poet:
sentences.i: and found it was a girl like a resplendent pearl, or a well-built dome, with a figure such as one would wish, of perfect height, with jutting breasts and rosy cheeks, as the poet said of her:
sentences.n: fa-wajadahā, “and he found her”: the pronoun now turns feminine. ka-, “like”, governs al-durra, and the dome (qubba) continues the comparison after aw, “or”. The rhymed prose (sajʿ) falls first in -iyya (saniyya, mabniyya, niyya), then in -add, -ahd, -add (qadd, nahd, khadd). بقامة النيّة is doubtful: niyya is “intention”, and “a stature of the intent” is taken here as “a stature such as one would intend or wish for”. A likely candidate is ألفيّة, alfiyya, “like the letter alif”, straight and slender, which keeps the rhyme; but the print is kept. The shaddas of المبنيّة, النيّة and مورّدة are the print's own. khumāsī, “five spans tall”, is said of a youth or girl of slender, well-grown height. khumāsiyyat al-qadd and the two phrases after it are adjectives annexed to a noun of the part: bārizat al-nahd, “prominent of breast”; muwarradat al-khadd, “rose-coloured of cheek”; all accusative, agreeing with ṣabiyyatan. kamā, “as”; fīhā, “about her”: the verses are applied to her as if made for her.

sentences.t:
اَرْبَعَةٌ مَا اجْتَمَعْنَ قَطُّ سِوَى * عَلَى اَذَى مُهْجَتِي وَسَفْكِ دَمِي
ضَوْءُ جَبِيْنٍ وَلَيْلُ سَالِفَةٍ * وَرْدُ خَدٍّ وَضَوْءُ مُبْتَسِمِ
sentences.tr:
arbaʿatun mā ijtamaʿna qaṭṭu siwā * ʿalā adhā muhjatī wa-safki damī
ḍawʾu jabīnin wa-laylu sālifatin * wardu khaddin wa-ḍawʾu mubtasimi
sentences.l:
Four (things) not they-came-together ever except * upon (the) harm (of) my-heart's-blood and-(the)-shedding (of) my-blood:
(the) light (of) a-brow, and-(the)-night (of) a-temple-lock, * (the) rose (of) a-cheek, and-(the)-light (of) a-smiling-(mouth).
sentences.i:
Four things have never once come together except to wound my heart and shed my blood:
the light of a brow, the night of a temple-lock, the rose of a cheek, and the light of a smile.
sentences.n: Metre: munsariḥ, rhyming in -mi. The pointing is the print's own. Line 1: arbaʿatun, “four”, takes the feminine plural verb ijtamaʿna, “they came together”, as things do. qaṭṭu, “ever”, after a negative. siwā ʿalā, “except against”: they have only ever united to harm him. muhja, “heart's blood”, the life itself. safk, “shedding”. Line 2 names the four: the bright brow; the sālifa, the lock of hair hanging at the temple, dark as night; the cheek, a rose; and the gleam of the mubtasim, the smiling mouth, its teeth flashing. The print points جَبِيْنٍ with a sukūn on the yā, as it often does a long vowel. wardu khaddin stands without wa-, “and”, and the hemistich is a syllable short for the munsariḥ: the metre wants wa-wardu, “and the rose”, as in the other three members, and the wa- has probably dropped out. The print is kept. The ء of ضوء is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَوْلُ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qawlu al-ākhari
sentences.l: And-(the)-saying (of) the-other:
sentences.i: And the words of another poet:
sentences.n: wa-qawlu al-ākhari, “and the saying of the other”, is a heading rather than a sentence: a second poem follows, as by another poet. The آ of الآخر is printed.

sentences.t:
بَدَتْ قَمَرًا وَمَالَتْ غُصْنَ بَانٍ * وَفَاحَتْ عَنْبَرًا وَرَنَتْ غِزَالًا
كَاَنَّ الْحُزْنَ مَشْغُوفٌ بِقَلْبِي * فَسَاعَةُ هَجْرِهَا يَجِدُ الْوِصَالَا
sentences.tr:
badat qamaran wa-mālat ghuṣna bānin * wa-fāḥat ʿanbaran wa-ranat ghizālan
ka-anna al-ḥuzna mashghūfun bi-qalbī * fa-sāʿatu hajrihā yajidu al-wiṣālā
sentences.l:
She-appeared (as) a-moon, and-swayed (as) a-bough (of) bān, * and-breathed (as) ambergris, and-gazed (as) a-gazelle.
As-if the-grief (is) passionately-in-love with-my-heart: * so-(the) hour (of) her-desertion, it-finds the-union.
sentences.i:
She rose a moon, swayed a bough of the bān tree, breathed ambergris, and gazed a gazelle.
It is as though grief were in love with my heart: in the hour she forsakes me, grief finds its union.
sentences.n: Metre: wāfir, rhyming in -ālā. The pointing is the print's own. Line 1: four verbs, each with an accusative of state (ḥāl) that says in what likeness she does it — a noun standing for “like a …”, the grammarians' stock example of a ḥāl that is a plain noun: badat qamaran, “she appeared as a moon”, mālat ghuṣna bānin, “she swayed as a bough of bān”, and so on. The bān is the ben tree (moringa), whose slender boughs stand for a supple figure. fāḥa, “to give off scent”; ranā, “to gaze fixedly”. The print points غِزَالًا with a kasra, ghizālan; the word for gazelle is ghazāl, and the print's vowel is kept. Line 2: كَاَنَّ is printed with a bare alif under the fatha: ka-anna, “as if”. mashghūf bi-, “smitten with”: shaghaf is love that reaches the shaghāf, the membrane round the heart, and bi- marks the beloved; so grief is the lover, and his heart its beloved. The print points فَسَاعَةُ in the nominative, sāʿatu, standing as a topic: “the hour of her desertion — then it finds union”; an adverb of time, sāʿata, would be the more usual. The point: grief meets its beloved, his heart, exactly when she leaves him. al-wiṣālā lengthens the rhyme vowel.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ بِنْتَ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ وَرَأَى حُسْنَهَا وَجَمَالَهَا وَهِيَ نَائِمَهْ بِجَانِبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā Qamaru al-Zamāni al-sitta Budūra binta al-maliki al-Ghayūri wa-raʾā ḥusnahā wa-jamālahā wa-hiya nāʾimah bi-jānibihi
sentences.l: So-when saw Qamar al-Zamān the-Lady Budūr, (the) daughter (of) the-King al-Ghayūr, and-saw her-beauty and-her-loveliness, and-she sleeping at-his-side,
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān saw the Lady Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr, and saw her beauty and loveliness as she lay asleep beside him,
sentences.n: The narrator names her; Qamar al-Zamān himself does not yet know who she is. al-sitt, “the lady”, is the colloquial title, set before the name. al-Ghayūr, “the Jealous”, is her father's name. The first راى is printed without its hamza (raʾā), as the edition often spells it; the second, رأى, has it. wa-hiya, “and she (was)”, brings in a circumstantial clause. نائمه is spelt with ه for ة and read pausally, nāʾimah; its ئ is printed. Budūr is a diptote and takes no tanwīn.

sentences.t: وَرَأَى عَلَيْهَا قَمِيصًا بُنْدُقِيًّا وَهِىَ بِلَا سِرْوَالٍ وَفَوْقَ رَأْسِهَا كُوفِيَّةٌ مُطَرَّزَةٌ بِالذَّهَبِ مُرَصَّعَةٌ بِالْجَوَاهِرِ وَفِي أُذُنَيْهَا زَوْجُ حَلَقٍ يُضِيءُ مِثْلَ الْكَوْكَبِ وَفِي عُنُقِهَا عِقْدٌ مِنَ الدُّرِّ الْيَتِيمِ لَايَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ أَحَدٌ مِنَ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: wa-raʾā ʿalayhā qamīṣan bunduqiyyan wa-hiya bi-lā sirwālin wa-fawqa raʾsihā kūfiyyatun muṭarrazatun bi-al-dhahabi muraṣṣaʿatun bi-al-jawāhiri wa-fī udhunayhā zawju ḥalaqin yuḍīʾu mithla al-kawkabi wa-fī ʿunuqihā ʿiqdun mina al-durri al-yatīmi lā-yaqdiru ʿalayhi aḥadun mina al-mulūki
sentences.l: and-saw on-her a-shift, Venetian, and-she (was) without drawers; and-above her-head a-coif embroidered with-the-gold, studded with-the-jewels; and-in her-two-ears a-pair (of) earrings shining like the-star; and-in her-neck a-necklace of the-pearls, the-orphan, not-has-power over-it anyone of the-kings;
sentences.i: and saw that she wore a Venetian shift and had no drawers on; on her head was a coif embroidered with gold and studded with jewels, in her ears a pair of earrings that shone like a star, and round her neck a necklace of matchless pearls such as no king could come by,
sentences.n: bunduqī, “Venetian”, from al-Bunduqiyya, Venice: a shift of fine imported stuff. وهى is spelt with ى for final ي. wa-hiya bi-lā sirwālin, “and she without drawers”: bi-lā, “with no”. The sirwāl, wide trousers, was worn under the shift, so beneath it she was naked. راسها is spelt without its hamza (raʾsihā). kūfiyya, a cap or coif. muṭarraz, “embroidered”, and muraṣṣaʿ, “inlaid, studded”: bi-, “with”, marks the material each time. zawj, “a pair”; ḥalaq, “earrings” (a collective). yuḍīʾu, “shines”, agrees with zawj; its ء is printed. al-durr al-yatīm, “the orphan pearls”: a pearl found alone in its shell, and so without peer. لايقدر is set solid in the print: lā yaqdiru ʿalayhi aḥadun, “no one has power over it”, no one could afford it; qadara takes ʿalā for what one is able to do or get. min, “of”, marks the class: “anyone among the kings”.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ إِلَيْهَا بِعَيْنِهِ فَصَارَ مَدْهُوشَ الْعَقْلِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ilayhā bi-ʿaynihi fa-ṣāra madhūsha al-ʿaqli
sentences.l: then-he-looked at-her with-his-eye, and-became bewildered (of) the-mind.
sentences.i: he looked at her with his own eyes, and his wits were dazed.
sentences.n: This answers fa-lammā raʾā, “when he saw”: fa-naẓara, “then he looked”. bi-ʿaynihi, “with his eye”: bi- marks the instrument; he saw her for himself. ṣāra, “to become”, takes its predicate in the accusative: madhūsha al-ʿaqli, “bewildered of mind”.

sentences.t: فَتَحَرَّكَتْ فِيهِ الْحَرَارَةُ الْغَرِيزِيَّةُ وَأَلْقَى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ شَهْوَةَ الْجِمَاعِ
sentences.tr: fa-taḥarrakat fīhi al-ḥarāratu al-gharīziyyatu wa-alqā Allāhu ʿalayhi shahwata al-jimāʿi
sentences.l: And-stirred in-him the-heat, the-innate, and-cast God upon-him (the) lust (of) the-intercourse.
sentences.i: The natural heat stirred in him, and God cast upon him the lust to couple with her.
sentences.n: al-ḥarāra al-gharīziyya, “the innate heat”, is a term of the old medicine, the body's vital heat; here it is plainly arousal. alqā ʿalā, “to cast upon”. shahwa, “lust, appetite”; jimāʿ, “sexual intercourse”, from jāmaʿa, literally “to come together with”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ مَاشَاءَ اللَّهُ كَانَ وَمَا لَمْ يَشَأْ لَمْ يَكُنْ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla fī nafsihi mā-shāʾa Allāhu kāna wa-mā lam yashaʾ lam yakun
sentences.l: And-he-said in himself: What-willed God was, and-what not He-willed not was.
sentences.i: He said to himself, “What God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not.”
sentences.n: qāla fī nafsihi, “he said in himself”, to himself. The pious formula takes the marvel as God's doing. ماشاء is set solid in the print. lam with the jussive: yashaʾ, with its أ printed, and yakun, from kāna.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ مَدَّ يَدَهُ إِلَيْهَا وَقَلَّبَهَا وَفَتَحَ طَوْقَ قَمِيصِهَا فَبَانَ لَهُ صَدْرُهَا وَرَأَى نُهُودَهَا مِثْلَ حُقَّيْنِ مِنَ الْعَاجِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu madda yadahu ilayhā wa-qallabahā wa-fataḥa ṭawqa qamīṣihā fa-bāna lahu ṣadruhā wa-raʾā nuhūdahā mithla ḥuqqayni mina al-ʿāji
sentences.l: Then indeed-he stretched his-hand to-her and-turned-her-over, and-opened (the) collar (of) her-shift; and-appeared to-him her-chest, and-he-saw her-breasts like two-caskets of the-ivory.
sentences.i: Then he put out his hand to her and turned her over, and opened the neck of her shift; her bosom lay bare to him, and he saw her breasts like two caskets of ivory.
sentences.n: thumma innahu, “then he”, the narrative's usual way of opening a new step. The shaddas of مدّ and قلّبها are the print's own. qallaba, Form II, “to turn over”. ṭawq, “collar, neck-opening”. bāna li-, “to become visible to”. nuhūd, plural of nahd, “breast”, used here of the pair. ḥuqq, a small round box or casket, in the dual, ḥuqqayni, genitive after mithla, “like”; min, “of”, gives the material.

sentences.t: فَازْدَادَ فِيهَا مَحَبَّةً وَرَغِبَ فِيهَا رَغْبَةً عَظِيمَةً فَصَارَ يُنَبِّهُهَا وَهِيَ لَا تَنْتَبِهُ لِأَنَّ دَهْنَشًا ثَقَّلَ نَوْمَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-izdāda fīhā maḥabbatan wa-raghiba fīhā raghbatan ʿaẓīmatan fa-ṣāra yunabbihuhā wa-hiya lā tantabihu li-anna Dahnashan thaqqala nawmahā
sentences.l: And-he-increased in-her (in) love, and-desired in-her a-desiring great; and-he-began rousing-her, and-she not waking, because Dahnash had-made-heavy her-sleep.
sentences.i: His love for her grew, and he desired her with a great desire. He began trying to rouse her, but she would not wake, for Dahnash had made her sleep heavy.
sentences.n: izdāda, Form VIII of zāda, “to increase”, with maḥabbatan, “in love”, an accusative saying in what. fī, “in”, marks the one loved, and raghiba fī, “to desire”, takes fī for what is wanted; raghbatan ʿaẓīmatan is the absolute object with an adjective, “a great desiring”. ṣāra with an imperfect is “began to”. nabbaha, Form II, “to wake someone”, and intabaha, Form VIII, “to wake up”; the shadda of ينبّهها is the print's own. li-anna, “because”: li-, “for”, with anna, “that”. ثقل is unpointed in the print; it is read thaqqala, Form II, “made heavy”, with Dahnash as its subject. Dahnashan again carries the printed alif of tanwīn.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَهُزُّهَا وَيُحَرِّكُهَا وَيَقُولُ يَا حَبِيبَتِي اسْتَيْقِظِي وَانْظُرِي مَنْ أَنَا فَأَنَا قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ فَلَمْ تَسْتَيْقِظْ وَلَمْ تُحَرِّكْ رَأْسَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra Qamaru al-Zamāni yahuzzuhā wa-yuḥarrikuhā wa-yaqūlu yā ḥabībatī istayqiẓī wa-unẓurī man anā fa-anā Qamaru al-Zamāni fa-lam tastayqiẓ wa-lam tuḥarrik raʾsahā
sentences.l: And-began Qamar al-Zamān shaking-her and-moving-her and-saying: O my-beloved, wake-up and-see who I (am), for-I (am) Qamar al-Zamān. But-not she-woke, and-not she-moved her-head.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān began to shake her and move her, saying, “My darling, wake up and see who I am: I am Qamar al-Zamān.” But she did not wake, nor so much as move her head.
sentences.n: The shaddas of يهزّها and يحرّكها are the print's own, and so is the fatha of مَن: man, “who”, not min, “from”. istayqiẓī and unẓurī are feminine imperatives: istayqaẓa, Form X, “to wake up”. fa-anā, “for I (am)”. lam with the jussive: tastayqiẓ, tuḥarrik. رأسها has its hamza printed here.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ تَفَكَّرَ فِي أَمْرِهَا سَاعَةً زَمَانِيَّةً وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِنْ صَدَقَ حَذْرِي فَهٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةُ هِىَ الَّتِي يُرِيدُ وَالِدِي زَوَاجِي بِهَا وَمَضَى لِي ثَلٰثُ سِنِينَ وَأَنَا أَمْتَنِعُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika tafakkara fī amrihā sāʿatan zamāniyyatan wa-qāla fī nafsihi in ṣadaqa ḥadhrī fa-hādhihi al-ṣabiyyatu hiya allatī yurīdu wālidī zawājī bihā wa-maḍā lī thalāthu sinīna wa-anā amtaniʿu min dhālika
sentences.l: So-at that he-pondered on her-affair an-hour of-time, and-said in himself: If proves-true my-guess, then-this the-girl, she (is) the-one-whom wants my-father my-marrying with-her; and-have-passed for-me three years, and-I refusing from that.
sentences.i: Then he pondered her case for a good while, and said to himself, “If my guess is right, this is the girl my father wants me to marry, and for three years now I have refused it.
sentences.n: sāʿa zamāniyya, “an hour of time”, is a stock phrase for “a good while”. ṣadaqa, “to be true, prove right”. حذري is doubtful. It is read here as ḥazr, “guess, estimate”, spelt with ذ for ز, as the two sounds fall together in everyday speech; the sense might also be ḥadhar, “wariness, misgiving”, as the letters stand. هى is spelt with ى for final ي. zawāj bi-, “marriage to”: as with tazawwaja bi-, bi- marks the bride. ثلث is the edition's spelling of thalāth, “three”, without the long alif, pointed with the dagger alif. maḍā lī, “has passed for me”: li- marks the one whose time goes by. wa-anā, “while I”, brings in the state. imtanaʿa min, “to hold back from, refuse”: min marks what is refused.

sentences.t: فَأَنَا إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ إِذَا جَاءَ الصُّبْحُ أَقُولُ لِأَبِي زَوِّجْنِى بِهَا لِأَ تَمَلَّى بِهَا وَالسَّلَامُ
sentences.tr: fa-anā in shāʾa Allāhu idhā jāʾa al-ṣubḥu aqūlu li-abī zawwijnī bihā li-a tamallā bihā wa-al-salāmu
sentences.l: So-I, if wills God, when comes the-morning, I-say to-my-father: Marry-me to-her, that-I-may-take-my-fill with-her; and-(that is) the-peace.
sentences.i: So, God willing, when morning comes I shall say to my father, ‘Marry me to her,’ so that I may take my fill of her, and there's an end of it.”
sentences.n: aqūlu, the imperfect, for the future: “I shall say”. li-, “to”, marks the one spoken to. zawwaja, Form II, “to give in marriage”, takes bi- for the bride: zawwijnī bihā, “marry me to her”. Its shadda is the print's own, and its final ى is the edition's ى for ي. لا تملى بها is doubtful. It is read here as one word split in two by the print's spacing, li-atamallā bihā, “that I may take my fill of her”: li-, “so that”, with the subjunctive, and tamallā, Form V, “to enjoy to the full”, which takes bi- for what is enjoyed, as in atamallā bi-wajhihā, “I feast my eyes on her face”, a few nights back. As the letters stand they could also be lā tumlī bihā, “do not keep me waiting for her”, from amlā, “to grant respite”, but that needs both a stretched sense and a long vowel after the prohibitive lā. wa-al-salām, “and peace”, closes a matter: “and that is all”. The ء of شاء and جاء is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
